newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan analysts cut GDP forecast on export shock.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan analysts cut GDP forecast on export shock.

text.p: Economic analysts said on Friday they would lower their 1996 Taiwan growth estimates after Taipei reported an unexpected fall in November export orders, including a striking downturn for information technology.

Foreign orders for Taiwan goods in November fell 4.16 percent to US$10.027 billion from November 1995 while November industrial output rose 3.22 percent from a year earlier, the economics ministry said on Friday.
"This has disappointed people," said Michael Hung, head of research at Nikko Securities.
"Exports were not so strong as expected and the government may not be able to reach its forecast of a 6.58 percent gross domestic product growth in the fourth quarter," Hung said.
Hung said Nikko planned to lower its fourth quarter GDP growth forecast to 6.3 percent from 6.5 percent.
Nikko's full-year 1996 GDP forecast would slip to 5.6 percent -- below the government's own relatively sober forecast of 5.7 percent for the year issued in November.
Nomura Securities also doubts the government's 6.58 percent fourth-quarter forecast, expecting only a 6.2 percent rise.
"It's not easy to see an expected major recovery due to unstable foreign orders performance but a gradual uptrend for industrial output is certain," said Nomura economist Amy Huang.
Officials nonetheless expressed optimism.

The ministry attributed November's decline in orders to an unusually high basis in 1995, when orders were peaking at exceptionally high levels -- due in good measure to the launch of Microsoft Corp's Windows 95 operating system.
The ministry said the fact that Taiwan's monthly export orders had exceeded $10 billion for four consecutive months would help contribute to steady future growth.

"Full-year 1996 export orders should still rise more than four percent to $118.9 billion and we expect the uptrend to continue in the first quarter of 1997," ministry statistics bureau director Chang Yao-tsung told reporters.

The worst news in the November export order data was a shock 19.24 percent decline in orders for information and telecommunication products at US$1.469 billion while orders for electronics fell 5.05 percent to $1.448 billion.

The downturn for Taiwan's most promising industrial sectors was most dramatic for orders from the United States, which fell 14.01 percent to $2.798 billion, pulled lower chiefly by smaller orders for information and telecom products, the ministry said.

Economists attributed the unexpected downturn in information technology orders to broad postponement of computer purchases as consumers await the expected introduction in 1997 of new models with higher-powered central processing units.

"Intel is expected to introduce its high-end CPUs with enhanced multimedia functions in 1997," said Hung of Nikko Securities. "Users have been waiting for this, thus delaying their purchases and making computer sales stagnant."

Despite the November fall in information and telecom product orders, the sector surged ahead in terms of output, enjoying a 22.47 percent growth in January-November and staking a claim as the main support for Taiwan's export growth, the ministry said.
Economists said that in order to achieve higher GDP growth, the government will have to rely more on boosting domestic demand rather than export growth.

"The recovery for exports will be slower than for domestic demand-oriented industries as the government has promised to boost domestic investment and accelerate public construction projects," Nomura's Huang said.
In November, industry output in the long-slumping property and construction industry fell a year-on-year 27.13 percent.
"This decline is a past indicator," Nikko's Hung said. "We should see a recovering real estate market soon following the finance ministry's successful state land auction."
The finance ministry said its Wednesday auction of 10 state land parcels went smoothly, with winning bids far higher than expected and almost double the base prices.
